text: The ark of the LORD was in Philistine territory seven months.
Then the Philistines summoned the priests and the diviners and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us how to send it back to its own place."

They answered, "If you send the ark of the God of Israel away, do not send it empty. By all means return a guilt offering to him. Then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand has not turned away from you."

"What guilt offering should we return to him?" they asked. They answered, "Five gold tumors and five gold mice, matching the number of the Philistine rulers, since the same plague struck all of you and your rulers.
Make images of your tumors and images of your mice that are ravaging the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand upon you, upon your gods, and upon your land.

versions.text: Make images of your tumors and images of the mice that are ravaging the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lift his hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has the possessive suffix on both nouns ("your tumors" and "your mice"). Keeping the parallel possessive preserves the rhetorical balance of the sentence and matches the source.

versions.text: Make images of your tumors and images of your mice that are ravaging the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lift his hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.
versions.explanation: The verb יָקֵל means "lighten, make light" rather than "lift, remove"; the Philistines hope for relief from the pressure of God's hand, and the preposition מֵעַל is idiomatically caught by "lighten his hand upon." "Lift his hand from" is a defensible dynamic rendering but loses the image of a weight being eased.

text: Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs? When he dealt harshly with them, did they not let the people go, and they went?
Now then, get a new cart ready, with two milk cows that have never worn a yoke. Hitch the cows to the cart, but take their calves away from them and shut them up at home.
Take the ark of the LORD and set it on the cart, and place beside it in a box the gold objects you are returning to him as a guilt offering. Then send it on its way,

and watch: if it goes up the road toward its own territory, toward Beth Shemesh, then it is the LORD who has brought this great disaster on us. But if it does not, then we will know it was not his hand that struck us; it happened to us by chance."
So the men did this. They took two milk cows and hitched them to the cart and shut their calves up at home.
They set the ark of the LORD on the cart, along with the box containing the gold mice and the images of their tumors.

Then the cows went straight up the road toward Beth Shemesh. They kept to the one highway, lowing as they went, and turned neither to the right nor to the left. The rulers of the Philistines followed them as far as the border of Beth Shemesh.
Now the people of Beth Shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. When they looked up and saw the ark, they rejoiced at the sight.
The cart came to the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stopped there beside a large stone. The people chopped up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.

The Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box that was with it, containing the gold objects, and set them on the large stone. That day the men of Beth Shemesh offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices to the LORD.
The five rulers of the Philistines saw all this and returned that same day to Ekron.
These are the gold tumors the Philistines sent back as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron.

And the gold mice matched the number of all the Philistine towns belonging to the five rulers—both the fortified cities and the outlying villages. The large stone on which they set the ark of the LORD is a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.[^1]

[^1]: The Hebrew text here reads "Abel the great"; the reading "the large stone" follows other ancient witnesses and matches verses 14–15.

versions.text: And the gold mice matched the number of all the Philistine towns belonging to the five rulers—both the fortified cities and the outlying villages. The large stone on which they set the ark of the LORD is a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.
versions.explanation: The rendering "large stone" reflects a textual variant (Hebrew "Abel" vs. "eben," stone). A brief footnote alerts the hearer/reader to the textual basis without disturbing the smooth oral reading.

text: But the LORD struck down some of the men of Beth Shemesh because they looked into the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy men out of fifty thousand, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck them with such a great blow.

versions.text: But God struck down some of the men of Beth Shemesh because they looked into the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy men out of fifty thousand, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck them with such a great blow.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew supplies no explicit subject for the first verb; the implied subject is the same one named later in the verse, "the LORD." Using "the LORD" throughout keeps the divine name consistent within the verse and avoids an unnecessary shift between "God" and "the LORD." A footnote noting that the Hebrew of the numbers here is difficult (literally "seventy men, fifty thousand men") would also help the reader.

text: The men of Beth Shemesh said, "Who can stand before the LORD, this holy God? To whom shall the ark go up from here?"
So they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath Jearim, saying, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to your place."
